profile.summary: 3 John is a short personal letter that reveals concrete tensions in the first churches: dispute for authority, rejection of apostolic leadership and the importance of Christian hospitality. The author, who identifies himself only as the priest, praises Gaius for his fidelity and acceptance of the messengers sent, while rebuking Diotrephes for his controlling behavior and for refusing John's authority. The letter also mentions Demetrius as someone of good reputation, possibly as a positive counterpoint to the example of Diotrephes. Although Christian tradition associates this letter with the apostle John, authorship and the exact date are not treated as absolutely certain in the introduction; in general, it is located in the same period of 1 and 2 John, probably at the end of the first century.
profile.setting: The letter was born amidst conflicts in the churches of Asia Minor, in a context in which some leaders judged themselves spiritual, but taught a stray Christology and rejected apostolic authority. Diotrephes appears as a local leader who departed from the apostolic communion, refusing the envoys of John and even excluding brothers who received them. John writes to Gaius to encourage him to remain firm in apostolic teaching and to continue demonstrating hospitality to the itinerant messengers. As for authorship, the letter is presented only as written by the "presbyter"; tradition identifies it with the apostle John, but this is presented as probable, not as absolute unanimity. The date is also approximate, usually located between 85 and 90 AD, in parallel with 1 and 2 John.

structure.label: Personal letter and leadership conflict
structure.description: A brief letter from the priest to Gaius, with praise for his faithfulness, warning against Diotrephes and mention of Demetrius as a figure of good testimony.

themes: Conflict and discipline in the community
readingKeys: Notice how the letter contrasts three characters: Gaius, Diotrephes and Demetrius, each representing a different posture to truth and communion.
Note the emphasis on hospitality: receiving the envoys of God is not social detail, but a concrete expression of loyalty to the gospel.
Read the letter thinking about the relationship between spiritual authority and service: the text criticizes the desire for control and values the conduct that cooperates with the apostolic work.
profile.cautions: The introduction does not allow to define with absolute certainty the authorship or date; the association with the apostle John and the chronology at the end of the first century are plausible but not incontestable traditions. It is also important not to turn Demetrius into a central character beyond what the letter tells: the introduction only says that he had a good reputation and may have served as a positive alternative to Diotrephes.

dossier.narratedEra: The letter is set in the lives of the Christian churches of the end of the first century, with the circulation of messengers/brothers between communities and tensions between local leaders and apostolic authority. The immediate scenario is that of a local church where Gáio receives hospitablely emissaries sent by John, while Diótrefes resists this apostolic network.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes place the composition in the same period of 1 and 2 John, probably around 85-90 AD, when John would be acting as an elder in Ephesus and in churches of Asia Minor. This date is presented as likely, not as absolute certainty.

politics.title: Contested apostolic authority
politics.detail: Diotrephes is described as one who rejects John's authority and refuses to receive the messengers sent by him; moreover, he expels from the church those who welcome them.
politics.readingImpact: The letter should be read as pastoral intervention in a concrete dispute of authority: it is not only moral exhortation, but a defense of the legitimacy of apostolic teaching and ecclesial communion.

politics.title: Break of communion with the apostolic circle
politics.detail: The notes link Diotrephes and his followers to dissent already treated in 1 John, as part of a movement that abandoned apostolic communion and taught different doctrine about Christ.
politics.readingImpact: The conflict is not only administrative; it is presented as a doctrinal and ecclesial separation that affects who is recognized as belonging to the truth.

politics.title: Network of churches and supervision of John
politics.detail: John writes hoping to regulate the conduct of a local church through emissaries and a future personal meeting, which shows an apostolic oversight relationship over scattered communities.
politics.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the letter is born from a relational structure between itinerant leader and local community, not an isolation of independent churches.

politics.title: Roman context of local circulation and leadership
politics.detail: The introduction points out that 3 John is a personal letter typical of the first century Greco-Roman world, in which letters served to maintain relationships and solve situations between people and groups.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read the text as a brief and practical intervention, with language of friendship, recommendation and honor, rather than systematic theological treatise.

customs.title: Hospitality for Christian travelers
customs.detail: Gáio is praised for receiving and hosting the brothers/shippers sent by John, and John encourages him to continue doing so.
customs.readingImpact: Hospitality appears as a concrete Christian duty and as a practical proof of fidelity to apostolic truth; the reader must note that welcoming messengers was equitable to cooperate with mission.

customs.title: Sustendad of missionaries by the churches
customs.detail: Travelers chose not to accept help from non-believers, depending on the support of the churches. The notes say that who sustains them becomes a partner of their work.
customs.readingImpact: The letter values the economy of the mission based on community support, so that receiving and financing missionaries is not secondary detail, but real participation in the work.

customs.title: Meal and implicit coexistence in hospitality
customs.detail: Although the letter does not describe meals, the aforementioned accommodation implies the use of domestic forms typical of old hospitality.
customs.readingImpact: The reader understands that fidelity manifests itself in the space of the house and of daily life; the text measures spirituality by domestic and community practices.

customs.title: Correspondence as a practice of communion
customs.detail: Matthew Henry points out that Christian communion is exercised and nourished by letter; Tyndale notes that 3 John follows the standard of old personal letter, with greeting, desire for well-being and closure.
customs.readingImpact: The epistle is read as a real means of relational government and pastoral encouragement, not just as a literary record.

customs.title: Aggressive local leadership and ecclesial discipline
customs.detail: Diotrephes is described as someone who exercises leadership inappropriately, rejecting apostolic envoys and expelling members who receive them.
customs.readingImpact: The text shows that the discipline of the church could be misused; the reader is warned not to confuse authority with personal dominion.

language.title: The elder" as self-presentation
language.detail: The author identifies himself only as an elder. The notes say that this may reflect age or authority before the recipients, and the ecclesiastical tradition identifies him with the apostle John.
language.readingImpact: The opening reinforces a personal and pastoral tone, at the same time humble and authoritative; the reader should not require a proper name to recognize the weight of the letter.

language.title: "Living according to the truth."
language.detail: The letter repeats the idea that Gáio walks in the truth, that is, remains faithful to the apostolic gospel of Christ.
language.readingImpact: It is not only correct opinion; it is practical fidelity to the apostolic teaching and the corresponding communion.

language.title: "By Love of the Name"
language.detail: The expression is explained as a reference to Jesus Christ, recognized by the early Christians without additional identification.
language.readingImpact: The reader perceives a reverent and shared way of speaking of Christ; the mission of the messengers is understood as a service directly linked to the Name of Jesus.

language.title: Contrast rhetorical between Gáio, Diotrefes and Demetrius
language.detail: The notes highlight that John uses moral contrast: Gáio is praised, Diotrephes is censored, and Demetrius is presented as a positive model and perhaps as a leadership alternative.
language.readingImpact: The reader should read the letter as a persuasive piece, built to form moral judgment through opposite examples.

language.title: Languages of old correspondence
language.detail: "Pen and ink" is explained as "ink and reed," and "face to face" as equivalent to a literal Greek expression "boca a boca."
language.readingImpact: These notes show that the letter belongs to the material world of ancient writing and uses idiomatisms that the modern reader needs to interpret with caution.

language.title: "Friends" as a category of communion
language.detail: The closure sends greeting the friends, defined in the notes as those who accept the apostolic gospel and live according to the truth.
language.readingImpact: The final word "amigos" works as a community mark, distinguishing who belongs to the apostolic fidelity network.

timeline.title: Same period of 1 and 2 John
timeline.detail: The letter is located at the same time of 1 and 2 John, with a probable composition between about 85-90 AD.
timeline.readingImpact: This guides the reading of 3 John as part of the same scenario of doctrinal and ecclesial conflicts already discussed in 1 John.

timeline.title: Final Decades of the First Century in Asia Minor
timeline.detail: The tradition presented in the notes locates John as an elder of the churches of Asia Minor in the last decades of the first century.
timeline.readingImpact: The background helps to understand why the letter deals with a network of churches, envoys and regional apostolic authority.

timeline.title: Ephesus as the Probable Base of the Letter
timeline.detail: The notes claim that the mentioned church was probably in Ephesus, where John would be staying.
timeline.readingImpact: The location suggests an important urban and missionary center, facilitating the sending of itinerant masters and correspondence with neighboring communities.

timeline.title: Context of dissent similar to that of 1 John
timeline.detail: The text was written after the emergence of teachers who claimed to be spiritual, taught another doctrine about Christ, and rejected the authority of the apostles.
timeline.readingImpact: The letter must be read in response to an already ongoing crisis, in which fidelity to Christ is inseparable from fidelity to the apostolic envoys.

timeline.title: Planned future visit of John
timeline.detail: At the close, John mentions the desire to visit soon and personally deal with the matter.
timeline.readingImpact: This shows that the letter is provisional and situational; it does not close the case, but it prepares a face-to-face intervention.

investigation: Gáio's exact identity is not clarified by the notes; they only say that there were several men with that name in the New Testament and the Greco-Roman world.
Demetrius' exact role remains uncertain: the note admits that we do not know safely why it is mentioned, although it suggests the possibility of being a leadership alternative in the community.
The expression "I have written to the church" in 3:9 is ambiguous in the notes: it may refer to 1 John or a letter today lost.
The location of the church in Ephesus is presented as the most likely, but not as absolute certainty.
The notes offer a traditional reading that identifies the elder with the apostle John; this identification is presented as a tradition of the church, not as an independent demonstration.

The sources provide few data on social classes, local economy, meals, formal cult or specific domestic structures; therefore these themes can only be mentioned when involved by the hospitality and support of missionaries.
dossier.limits: This dossier was built only with the attached notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry, without resorting to external data. Therefore, coverage is selective: there is strong emphasis on leadership, hospitality, apostolic authority and the circulation of messengers, but almost no direct information about civil government, empires, social classes, work or detailed liturgy. Where the notes only suggest something, this was classified as interpretation; where they mention uncertainty, I preserved ambiguity. The tradition that identifies the author with the apostle John appears in the notes, but remains as tradition and not as an independent historical proof. Similarly, the date of 85-90 AD. is likely according to the source, not a closed chronology. No events from other books have been mixed, except when the notes themselves make explicit comparison with 1 and 2 John or with references from the New Testament to clarify terms and practices.
